cf.title: Delete GIN posting-tree pages without excessive locking

input.subject: Delete GIN posting tree pages without excessive locking

verdict_reasoning: Level 1b fails on demand-1. Message #1 names no current workload that stalls behind the root cleanup lock, and it says the 2016 case was solved by what remained after fd83c83d094. The author asks whether anyone is interested, and nobody has replied. This is a "not now, show demand" result; the design objections at level 2 were not evaluated.

brief.title: Delete empty GIN posting tree pages without locking out the tree
brief.problem: Vacuum deletes empty posting tree pages in a second pass that holds a cleanup lock on the tree root for the whole pass. This blocks all searches and insertions into that posting tree, and the pass cannot be interrupted. The author does not name current users who suffer from this; the original case was Yandex.Mail folder search in 2016.
brief.proposed_design: Vacuum deletes empty leaf pages during its normal left-to-right sweep of the leaf level, using lock coupling in the same order as stepping right. It finds the parent by walking right one level above the leaves and deletes a page only if no other backend holds a pin on it. Internal pages, the leftmost and rightmost leaves, and leaves under a parent's last downlink are never deleted.
user_visible_surface: No SQL, GUC, catalog or C API change; the patch touches only ginbtree.c, ginvacuum.c and the GIN README.
New injection points in the GIN vacuum sweep, used by new isolation tests in src/test/modules/gin.
author_claims: Searches and insertions into a posting tree proceed while vacuum is paused mid-sweep.
Vacuum and insertions both lock leaf-to-parent and left-to-right, so they cannot form a lock cycle.
Inserters that follow a stale downlink to a deleted page recover by moving right; existing XID stamping prevents early page reuse.
The 0003 deadlock provocation tests would hang if the locking protocol regressed.
amcheck for GIN and injection points make getting this right easier than in 2016-2018.
brief.thread_state: Only the first message is visible, and nobody has replied. The author asks whether anyone is interested, and CFbot reports the patch needs a rebase.
unclear: No performance or concurrency numbers, before or after.
Whether empty internal pages and pinned empty leaves now accumulate, since the patch never deletes them, and how much bloat this leaves.
What changes in WAL records and replay for page deletion, and whether hot standby readers stay safe.
How the new protocol differs from the 2016 optimizations reverted in fd83c83d094, and why it avoids their bug.
Whether the README hunk fully explains the inserter-side recovery, since it is truncated here.

objections.title: No current user is shown to suffer from the root cleanup lock
objections.failure_scenario: A committer takes on a new posting-tree deletion protocol in GIN vacuum. No workload is known to be blocked by the second pass today, so the change has no measured benefit, and users only meet its risk.
objections.argument: Message #1 says the only known case, Yandex.Mail in 2016, was solved by what remained after fd83c83d094. It offers to continue only "if anyone actually suffers from this". The thread has no replies, no field reports and no numbers on how long the root cleanup lock blocks searches. A reference to another thread that "reminded" the author is not a report of a user problem.
objections.author_must_show: Which current workloads see searches or inserts stalled behind the posting-tree deletion pass, and for how long, on which index sizes?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 asks whether anyone suffers from this and says the 2016 case was solved by what remained after the revert. The thread has no replies, field reports or stall measurements, so demand is not shown.

other_surviving.title: No account of how this avoids the bug behind the earlier revert
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A committer pushes the new deletion protocol. A concurrency flaw of the same kind that forced the 2016 revert shows up later as a corrupt posting tree or wrong search results under concurrent vacuum and insert. Users find it after release, and amcheck reports it only after the damage.
other_surviving.argument: Message #1 says the 2016 GIN locking work "turned out to be incorrect" and most of it was reverted in fd83c83d094, and this patch comes from the same effort. The material does not say what was wrong then, or which invariant the new protocol keeps that the old one broke. The README hunk explains the new protocol, but it does not compare it with the reverted one. New tests and amcheck help, but they only cover the cases someone thought to test, so a committer would likely ask for the comparison first.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What exactly was incorrect in the locking reverted by fd83c83d094, and which part of the new protocol rules out that failure?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 says the earlier fix was incorrect and was reverted in fd83c83d094, but it does not say what the flaw was. The visible README text describes the new protocol only, so the comparison is missing.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Standby replay gets no equivalent of the primary-side pin check
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A hot standby scan pins posting tree leaf 'f', copies its items, and will return to it. On the primary, vacuum sees no pin on 'f' and deletes it. The startup process then replays the deletion on the standby while the standby scan still holds its pin, so the scan returns to a page that is now marked deleted.
other_surviving.argument: The README says a pin means a scan "has copied the page's contents and may yet return to it", and deletion skips such pages for that reason. That check runs only on the primary and cannot see standby pins. Until now the root cleanup lock on the primary limited how deletion ran. The patch does not touch ginxlog.c, and message #1 does not say how page-deletion replay keeps standby scans safe or in what order replay locks the pages.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How does replay of a posting tree page deletion stay safe for a hot standby scan that holds a pin on the deleted leaf, and does replay take locks in left-to-right order?

critic.reasoning: The patch does not touch ginxlog.c, so the standby exposure may be the same as today, when the root cleanup lock also exists only on the primary. The material does not say this, and the new pin rule makes the question fair.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Empty internal and last-downlink pages are never reclaimed
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user deletes a large old range of rows, which empties whole subtrees of a posting tree. Today the second pass removes the empty internal pages. With the patch, internal pages, leaves under each parent's last downlink and pinned leaves stay. Every later scan walks these empty pages, and the index never shrinks back.
other_surviving.argument: The removed README text shows the current algorithm deleting internal page 'c' once it has no downlinks. The new protocol never deletes internal pages, and it skips some leaves by design. Every GIN user gets this change, including the large majority who never see the lock stall. The proposal gives no numbers on how much reclaim is lost, so the cost may fall on users who gain nothing from the change.
other_surviving.author_must_show: After a mass delete, how much posting-tree space does the patch leave unreclaimed compared with the current two-pass deletion, and how does that affect scan cost?

critic.reasoning: The removed README text shows the current code deleting an empty internal page, and the new protocol never does. The last-downlink rule keeps at least one leaf per parent, which may bound the loss, but the proposal gives no numbers.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: Subtle new locking protocol with no shown users and no engaged owner
refuted.failure_scenario: A later change to GIN split or stepping-right logic breaks an assumption the sweep relies on, such as the lock order or the stale-downlink recovery. The result is a rare deadlock or a lost-page corruption, found in production long after commit. Few people know GIN locking well enough to diagnose it.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says the author will continue only "if anyone actually suffers from this", and it names no current user, only a 2016 case already solved by what remained after fd83c83d094. Earlier GIN locking work in this same area had to be reverted, which the author says himself. No committer has replied, and CFbot shows the patch needs a rebase. A committer would likely ask who owns this protocol before taking on the liability of a concurrency change that has no demonstrated users.
refuted.author_must_show: Which current workloads see searches or inserts stall behind the root cleanup lock, and which committer familiar with GIN locking will review and own the protocol?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1 for the demand part. The missing owner is a committability matter, which the rubric says must not raise the verdict, and the failure scenario names no concrete broken assumption.

refuted.title: Every GIN user carries the locking risk for a narrow gain
refuted.failure_scenario: After release, a corner case in the new leaf-deletion protocol causes a hang or a corrupt posting tree during routine vacuum on an ordinary GIN index. The owner of an index that never had a stall problem finds out from a failed query or an amcheck report.
refuted.argument: The patch replaces the deletion path for every GIN posting tree, so the whole user base is exposed to the risk of a new concurrency protocol. Message #1 states that earlier locking work in this exact area was incorrect and was reverted. The benefit goes only to workloads with large posting trees, many empty pages and concurrent access during vacuum. Message #1 does not size that group.
refuted.author_must_show: How large is the group that gains from this, and why does that gain justify new concurrency risk on every GIN index?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1 for the size of the group that gains. The risk part names no concrete flaw in the protocol and would fit any concurrency change; maintenance-fit-2 covers the concrete cost to non-users.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: Page deletion now runs without the root cleanup lock, and replay on a hot standby cannot see the primary's pin check.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A new posting tree deletion protocol in ginvacuum.c and ginbtree.c that later GIN locking changes must keep intact.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The patch changes ginbtree.c, which insertions and searches use, and leaves some empty pages for later scans to walk.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: Message #1 shows no current user who needs the change.

questions: Which current workloads see searches or insertions stall behind the posting tree deletion pass, for how long, and on which index sizes?
What was incorrect in the locking reverted by fd83c83d094, and which part of the new protocol rules out that failure?
How does replay of a posting tree page deletion stay safe for a hot standby scan that holds a pin on the deleted leaf?
After a mass delete, how much posting tree space stays unreclaimed compared with the current two-pass deletion, and what does that cost later scans?
What do before and after measurements show for search and insertion latency during vacuum of a large posting tree?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows GIN posting tree locking, page deletion and its WAL replay. Nobody has replied to message #1.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a new concurrency protocol on every GIN index, with no end date. Message #1 says earlier locking work in this area was incorrect and was reverted.
committability.author_follow_up: Message #1 offers further work only "if anyone actually suffers from this". The author moved the entry to the next CommitFest, but the rebase that CFbot asked for is still open.

not_now.evidence_that_would_change_it: A report from at least one current workload where searches or insertions stall behind the root cleanup lock, with stall times and index sizes. A reproducible benchmark that shows the stall before the patch and its absence after would also count.

priority.reason: The patch adds no user-visible surface, but the locking protocol needs care for ever and expert review of GIN concurrency. No current user is shown and nobody has replied, so it can wait until someone reports the stall.

provisional_note: The code and the truncated part of the README were not read, so lock ordering, inserter recovery and WAL replay are unchecked. Three level 2 objections survived (prior-attempts-1, replication-ondisk-1, maintenance-fit-2) and remain open.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Predicate locking in Gin index
precedents_retrieved.summary: A GSoC 2017 patch adding explicit predicate locking to the GIN index access method for serializable isolation, placing page-level predicate locks on entry tree and posting tree leaf pages and copying locks on page splits. It also handled conflict detection when fast update is enabled.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewer Alexander Korotkov found the locking scheme redundant and asked for changes: lock posting tree leaves instead of entry tree leaves, apply page-level locks only when fast update is off, add in-code comments, and improve the isolation tests so they actually create posting trees. After his last review the thread had no updates for almost two months, and Michael Paquier marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This thread had no updates for almost two months, so I am marking it
as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Predicate locking in gin index
precedents_retrieved.summary: A GSoC 2017 patch adds explicit predicate locking to the GIN index access method so that serializable transactions detect rw-conflicts at page level. When fast update is on, the patch falls back to coarser locking.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund closed the entry as a duplicate of an older commitfest entry (1466), so it was not rejected on technical grounds. Before that, Michael Paquier had marked it returned with feedback after about two months with no update. Alexander Korotkov's review asked for consistent fast-update conditions, code comments, and isolation tests that build a posting tree.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This appears to be a duplicate of https://commitfest.postgresql.org/17/1466/ - as the other one is older, I'm closing this one.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
Reverted commit(s): Compress GIN posting lists, for smaller index size.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 36a35c55 changed the divisor from 3 to 6, for no apparent reason.
Reducing GinMaxItemSize like that created a dump/reload hazard: loading a
9.3 database to 9.4 might fail with "index row size XXX exceeds maximum 1352
for index ..." error. Revert the change.

While we're at it, make the calculation slightly more accurate. It used to
divide the available space on page by three, then subtract
sizeof(ItemIdData), and finally round down. That's not totally accurate; the
item pointers for the three items are packed tight right after the page
header, but there is alignment padding after the item pointers. Change the
calculation to reflect that, like BTMaxItemSize does. I tested this with
different block sizes on systems with 4- and 8-byte alignment, and the value
after the final MAXALIGN_DOWN was the same with both methods on all
configurations. So this does not make any difference currently, but let's be
tidy.

Also add a comment explaining what the macro does.

This fixes bug #12292 reported by Robert Thaler. Backpatch to 9.4, where the
bug was introduced.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert the commits related to allowing page lock to conflict among parallel group members.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert the commits related to allowing page lock to conflict among parallel group members.
Reverted commit(s): Allow page lock to conflict among parallel group members.; Add assert to ensure that page locks don't participate in deadlock cycle.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts the work done by commits 3ba59ccc89 and 72e78d831a.
Those commits were incorrect in asserting that we never acquire any other
heavy-weight lock after acquring page lock other than relation extension
lock. We can acquire a lock on catalogs while doing catalog look up after
acquring page lock.

This won't impact any existing feature but we need to think some other way
to achieve this before parallelizing other write operations or even
improving the parallelism in vacuum (like allowing multiple workers
for an index).

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
Reverted commit(s): Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 2aa6e33, that added a fast path to skip
anti-wraparound and non-aggressive autovacuum jobs (these have no sense
as anti-wraparound implies aggressive).  With a cluster using a high
amount of relations with a portion of them being heavily updated, this
could cause autovacuum to lock down, with autovacuum workers attempting
repeatedly those jobs on the same relations for the same database, that
just kept being skipped.  This lock down can be solved with a manual
VACUUM FREEZE.

Justin King has reported one environment where the issue happened, and
Julien Rouhaud and I have been able to reproduce it in a second
environment.  With a very aggressive autovacuum_freeze_max_age,
triggering those jobs with pgbench is a matter of minutes, and hitting
the lock down is a lot harder (my local tests failed to do that).

Note that anti-wraparound and non-aggressive jobs can only be triggered
on a subset of shared catalogs:
- pg_auth_members
- pg_authid
- pg_database
- pg_replication_origin
- pg_shseclabel
- pg_subscription
- pg_tablespace
While the lock down was possible down to v12, the root cause of those
jobs is a much older issue, which needs more analysis.

Bonus thanks to Andres Freund for the discussion.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fixes a trivial bug in dumped parse/query/plan trees
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the leading space that the node output code writes after the opening parenthesis when it dumps an array field, so "( 1 4)" becomes "(1 4)". The author called the space a bug in the dumped parse, query and plan trees.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Daniel Gustafsson and Tom Lane said the format is intentional and that changing it could break external parsers of the node format. Tom Lane said the space is a skipped minor optimization and that a small saving in isolation does not justify the risk to third-party code. He would accept such breakage only for a large cut in stored parse tree size, about 2X or better.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
While our existing nodeRead code wouldn't have a
problem with removing the extra whitespace, I share your fear that
we could introduce bugs into some third-party code somewhere.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add OID descriptions to dumped parse/query/plan trees
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds comments to the text dumps of parse, query and plan trees that name the object behind each OID, such as the index, operator, function or type. It does this by catalog lookups inside the node output code.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the lookups would make the dump code need a live, non-aborted transaction and could add catalog accesses that cause problems or deadlocks, so pprint could no longer be called from almost anywhere. He also said the change breaks re-reading of dumped trees, which rules, views and parallel query depend on. The author withdrew the patch after this reply.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It means that the dump code has to
execute in a live (not-aborted) transaction, which is not a
requirement it had before, and will complicate some debugging
scenarios.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance
Reverted commit(s): VACUUM: ignore indexing operations with CONCURRENTLY
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit d9d076222f5b "VACUUM: ignore indexing operations
with CONCURRENTLY".

These changes caused indexes created with the CONCURRENTLY option to
miss heap tuples that were HOT-updated and HOT-pruned during the index
creation.  Before these changes, HOT pruning would have been prevented
by the Xmin of the transaction creating the index, but because this
change was precisely to allow the Xmin to move forward ignoring that
backend, now other backends scanning the table can prune them.  This is
not a problem for VACUUM (which requires a lock that conflicts with a
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY operation), but HOT-prune can definitely
occur.  In other words, Xmin advancement was sped up, but at the cost of
corrupting the resulting index.

Regrettably, this means that the new feature in PG14 that RIC/CIC on
very large tables no longer force VACUUM to retain very old tuples goes
away.  We might try to implement it again in a later release, but for
now the risk of indexes missing tuples is too high and there's no easy
fix.

Backpatch to 14, where this change appeared.

Diagnosys-by: Andrey Borodin <x4mmm@yandex-team.ru>
Diagnosys-by: Michael Paquier <michael@paquier.xyz>
Diagnosys-by: Andres Freund <andres@anarazel.de>

precedents_retrieved.title: KNN for B-tree
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set adds kNN search to B-tree so that `ORDER BY col <-> const LIMIT k` can use a B-tree index, with a bidirectional scan that starts at the target value and moves toward the nearer next tuple. It also changes the planner interface for index ordering, adds core distance operators for scalar types to the B-tree opclasses, and removes the duplicate operators from btree_gist.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Alexander Korotkov, the reviewer preparing it for commit, decided the implementation was in the wrong place and marked it returned with feedback, suggesting a new implementation for v14. The patch merges a forward and a backward scan inside the B-tree code, but that merge belongs in the IndexScan node or the optimizer and executor. The other approach he named is a priority-queue scan in B-tree like GiST and SP-GiST, which needs much more work in the B-tree core. In 2017 the patch had been returned once before because the amcanorderbyop redesign needed more thought.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The appropriate place to do this high-level work is IndexScan node or even Optimizer/Executor (Merge node over to IndexScan nodes), but not B-tree itself.

precedents_retrieved.title: btree_gin and ranges
precedents_retrieved.summary: Teodor Sigaev proposed adding support in btree_gin for the range 'contained by' operator (<@) over scalar columns, for int4, int8, numeric, date and timestamp types. This lets a range condition such as i <@ '[-1,1]'::int4range be answered with a single GIN scan instead of two half-open scans.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Early on, Marti Raudsepp asked whether this should be implemented more generically, since plain btree could also support <@ and btree_gin's behavior would diverge from btree. Heikki Linnakangas then refactored the module, rebased the patch and asked for more comments, and the author posted a revised, split patch. The thread ends there, with no recorded objection or decision.

precedents_retrieved.title: DELETE CASCADE
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a `DELETE CASCADE` statement that treats existing NO ACTION and RESTRICT foreign keys as CASCADE for that one statement. The goal is to delete rows with dependents without redefining the constraints.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stopped applying, and the author did not reply for about four months, so Julien Rouhaud closed it under the commitfest rules. The design was still open. David G. Johnston preferred making FK actions changeable with ALTER CONSTRAINT, and Tom Lane suggested `SET CONSTRAINTS ... ON DELETE referential_action`, which names the constraints explicitly. Julien said the feature itself is wanted and a resubmission is expected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It's been almost 4 months since your last email, and almost 2 weeks since the notice that this patch doesn't apply anymore.

precedents_retrieved.title: use AV work items infrastructure for GIN pending list's cleanup
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves GIN pending list cleanup to an autovacuum work item, requested when the list reaches gin_pending_list_limit. Inserts and updates would then no longer pay for the cleanup.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Masahiko Sawada pointed out that work items run only after an autovacuum run, so the pending list could grow far past gin_pending_list_limit while the same work item is registered again and again. He suggested a soft limit and a hard limit, removal of duplicate work items, and skipping the item if autovacuum already cleaned the index. The author had no time to finish a revised version, so he marked the entry "Returned with feedback" and planned to resubmit.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So if many insertions happen before executing the autovacuum
work item, we will end up greatly exceeding the threshold
(gin_pending_list_limit) and registering the same work item again and
again.

precedents_retrieved.title: Retail IndexTuple Deletion
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Retail IndexTuple Deletion
Threads: [WIP] [B-Tree] Retail IndexTuple deletion

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent matches. [P4] (GiST page deletion) and [P20] (btree vacuum replay) have no recorded reason, so neither supports an objection. The only prior attempt is the reverted 2016 work that message #1 names.

The patch changes no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog, psql command or client-visible behaviour, so pg_dump round-trip and driver compatibility are not affected. WAL record changes, standby safety and on-disk effects of the new deletion rules belong to other angles and need the code to check.
The patch changes no on-disk format, catalog, wire protocol or C API, and the touched files suggest the WAL record format is unchanged, so pg_upgrade and mixed-version replication are not affected.

The proposal changes only internal GIN vacuum locking. It adds no SQL, GUC, catalog, privilege or monitoring surface, and no new information path, so it gives no user access they lacked before. An open scan's pin can delay deleting a page, which is a bloat or correctness question for the design angle. I found no privilege concern.
Two objections raised. Hot-path cost for insertions and searches could not be judged without code or measurements, and the proposal includes neither.

No existing feature or extension removes the root cleanup lock during posting tree page deletion, because this is internal to GIN vacuum and no hook can reach it. Skipping index cleanup with VACUUM (INDEX_CLEANUP off) avoids the lock but stops removing dead TIDs, so it does not do the same job.
Two demand objections are raised. Both are "not now, show demand" points, and neither is a rejection of the design.
